title: 1.1 Introduction to Algorithms, Programming, and Compilers

content.value: Describe algorithms, inputs, and outputs; distinguish syntax, run-time, and logic errors; trace and test a short program.

Programming turns a problem specification into executable instructions. First identify what data is supplied, what result is required, and any constraints on valid input. Design a precise algorithm, express it in code, then test it against expected results. These steps are iterative: a failed test can reveal a mistake in the design as well as in the code.

Java source code is compiled into bytecode that a Java runtime can execute. The compiler checks grammar and type rules. It cannot determine whether your formula matches the problem. Separate language errors, failures during execution, and incorrect results produced by otherwise valid code. An IDE (integrated development environment) combines an editor with tools for compiling, running, and debugging programs. An exception interrupts normal execution when a run-time problem occurs.

The state begins with tickets = 3 and price = 8. Multiplication produces 24, which is stored in total and printed. The algorithm is: obtain a count and price, multiply them, and report the product. This algorithm can also be described without Java. In this first example, focus on the input values, the calculation, and the output. The class and main-method wrapper lets Java run the example; its declaration details are taught in later topics.

Replacing * with + is a logic error: the code still compiles, but prints 11. Missing a semicolon is a syntax error. Test zero tickets, one ticket, and several tickets; expected results follow from the specification.
Change tickets to 0 and predict the output before running it. Answer: 0. Explain why this boundary case is useful and why compiling successfully does not guarantee every case works.
